label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **the Nasdaq fell 2.6 percent, its worst day since June**, on AI funding fears and oil, and the S&P 500 lost 1.2 percent (CNBC). Oil sits near $100 and **Brent hit a five-month high** after the New York Times reported U.S. and Israeli plans for new Iran strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms (CNBC, Fox News). Trump says the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran, and Washington pulled non-emergency staff from Saudi Arabia (CNBC). Polls from Fox News, CNN and NPR **put Democrats ahead for the midterms**, with Trump's approval at 32 to 36 percent (Fox News, CNN, NPR). In California, the Justice Department wants courts to stop the counting of ballots tied to **20,000 flagged registrants**, and the state says many were never mailed ballots (Fox News, SF Chronicle, CalMatters). State workers staged their first one-day strike, with mediation due Oct. 30 (CalMatters). Putin agreed in principle to resume three-way Ukraine talks after Nov. 10 (The Hill), while Kyiv was hit hours later (CNN). Tesla beat estimates and Musk said SpaceX and Tesla are discussing a merger (CNBC). Merck and Moderna's mRNA vaccine **cut melanoma recurrence risk 42 percent** (CNN), and NASA briefs on Artemis III at 2 p.m. ET (Space.com).

alerts.text: Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 and Amazon Oct. 29 after the close, and all three fell 2 to 5 percent in the latest data.
A federal judge and the Ninth Circuit could rule any day on whether California must set aside ballots tied to 20,000 flagged voters.
NASA's Artemis III briefing is at 2 p.m. ET (11 a.m. Pacific) today.
An early, mutated flu strain is spreading on the West Coast, so consider booking a flu shot (CNN).

highlights.text: Nasdaq sinks 2.6 percent, its worst day since June, as AI funding fears and oil bite.
Oil jumps on reports of U.S.-Israeli Iran strike plans after the midterms.
Fox, CNN and NPR polls put Democrats ahead; Trump approval 32 to 36 percent.
DOJ asks courts to block counting 20,000 California ballots; state disputes the list.
Merck-Moderna mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk 42 percent.

markets.wrap: The Nasdaq fell 2.60 percent to 26,008.86, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 lost 1.21 percent as **AI funding worries and oil above $100** hit tech (CNBC). Futures stayed lower Thursday night (CNBC). Tesla beat estimates but slid on spending concerns, and SpaceX rose 10 percent after Musk floated a merger (CNBC). Brent hit a five-month high on reports of planned Iran strikes (CNBC, Fox News).

stories.title: Polls show Democrats ahead for the Nov. 3 midterms
stories.summary: Fox, CNN and NPR polls all put Democrats ahead on the House ballot and Trump's approval near record lows.
story: A Fox News poll taken Oct. 9-12 puts Trump's approval at 36 percent, the lowest in any Fox survey of his two terms, and shows Democrats ahead 54 to 45 on the House ballot (Fox News). Approval among Republicans fell to 76 percent in that poll. The Washington Examiner also reported a new low for Trump's approval despite his campaign push.

Other pollsters see the same shape. A CNN/SSRS poll from Oct. 15-18 has Democrats up 49 to 39 on the congressional ballot, the widest margin in that poll since just before the 2020 election, with Trump at 32 percent approval (CNN). NPR's poll of Oct. 13-19 found likely voters preferring a Democrat 54 to 42 and Trump at 34 percent approval, 62 percent disapproval (NPR). The Hill summarized the trend as a 10-point Democratic edge.

The Senate is tighter. CNN's poll averages show Maine at 49 to 48 for Democrat Troy Jackson over Susan Collins, Ohio at 49 to 44 for Sherrod Brown over Jon Husted, and Michigan at 49 to 47 for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed over Mike Rogers. An Emerson poll has Texas at 48 to 46 for Democrat James Talarico over Ken Paxton, inside the margin of error (The Hill).

Republicans say the polls can be beaten. Fox's Republican co-pollster Daron Shaw said the party still has time to close gaps, though it is getting late, and conservative commentators argue that the Democratic Party's leftward drift gives the GOP an opening with moderates (Fox News).
facts: Fox News poll, Oct. 9-12: Trump approval 36%, a record low in Fox polling.
Same poll: Democrats lead the House ballot 54% to 45%.
CNN/SSRS, Oct. 15-18: Democrats 49%, Republicans 39%; Trump approval 32%.
NPR poll, Oct. 13-19: likely voters prefer a Democrat 54% to 42%.
Election Day is Nov. 3.
stories.next: Early voting is under way; watch fresh polls from NYT/Siena and Emerson before Nov. 3.
stories.left: Voters are telling every pollster the same thing: costs are too high and they want a check on the president. With Trump below 40 percent in every major survey, Democrats argue the House is theirs to win and the Senate is in play. They say the fight over election rules shows an administration worried about the result.
stories.right: Polls are snapshots, and conservatives note that midterm electorates differ from poll samples. Republicans say Democratic primary wins by left-wing candidates let them paint the whole party as extreme, and they point to strong fundraising and Speaker Johnson's confidence that the majority holds. A late swing among low-propensity voters could narrow the gap.

stories.title: Justice Department asks courts to block counting of 20,000 California ballots
stories.summary: DOJ says all 20,000 people it flagged are noncitizens; California says its own sample shows many were never mailed ballots.
story: The Justice Department sued California on Oct. 15 in Los Angeles federal court, asking the court to bar officials from counting mail ballots tied to about 20,000 registrants it calls likely noncitizens, or to force the state to verify their citizenship first (Fox News, SF Chronicle). Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in the Central District, said investigators reviewed every name and concluded all 20,000 are noncitizens who likely received ballots (Fox News).

California disputes the list. Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote that the administration listed people it "believes" are "likely" noncitizens, and a Los Angeles County official said that in a 200-record sample, 112 matched canceled or inactive registrations that were not mailed ballots (SF Chronicle, CalMatters). The county also said it lacks the data to verify citizenship.

Judge David Carter scheduled a hearing on the emergency request, and DOJ then asked the Ninth Circuit to step in before he ruled (The Hill). Prosecutors separately charged 28 green-card holders from the list with illegal voting (CalMatters). Newsom called the suit an attempt to make California "violate federal law" (Fox News).
Election lawyers told the SF Chronicle they had never seen anything like the suit. I found no ruling yet from Carter or the Ninth Circuit.
facts: DOJ filed suit Oct. 15 in Los Angeles federal court.
The list has about 20,000 registrants DOJ calls likely noncitizens.
LA County's sample found 112 of 200 records tied to canceled or inactive registrations.
DOJ charged 28 green-card holders from the list.
No ruling has been reported.
stories.next: A ruling from Judge Carter or the Ninth Circuit could land any day; ballots are being counted through Nov. 3 and after.
stories.left: Democrats and California officials say the list is unreliable and that sweeping the ballots of tens of thousands of registrants, some never mailed a ballot, risks disenfranchising citizens days before an election. They call threats of criminal charges against election workers intimidation and note that courts have repeatedly rejected the DOJ's voter-roll demands.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that counting ballots from noncitizens would dilute citizens' votes, and that the 28 criminal charges show the problem is real. They say federal agencies hold the immigration records counties lack, and that a state refusing to cooperate with a federal check invites distrust in the result.
stories.flag: Essayli's claim that every name is a verified noncitizen has not been independently confirmed; California disputes it.

stories.title: California state workers stage first-ever one-day strike
stories.summary: About 100,000 SEIU Local 1000 members fought over pay, health costs and Newsom's office mandate; mediation resumes Oct. 30.
story: Thousands of California state workers walked off the job on Oct. 21 in a one-day strike by SEIU Local 1000, the first in the union's history, over pay, health care costs and remote-work rules (CalMatters, AP). The union represents about 100,000 state employees, and its contract expired June 30. Some DMV, parks and other services were limited (CalMatters).

Members voted 96.2 percent to authorize the strike. The union says the state is bargaining in bad faith, and the state labor board sided with it, finding that CalHR refused to meet and confer in good faith (CalMatters). The state's human resources department says it "remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement."

Both sides are due back in mediation Oct. 30, and the union has said it could escalate if talks stall (CalMatters). The dispute lands in Gov. Newsom's final months in office and centers on his four-day in-office requirement and state health contributions.
Newsom earlier vetoed a bill that would have given striking workers unemployment benefits (Fox Business).
facts: The strike took place Oct. 21 and lasted one day.
SEIU Local 1000 represents about 100,000 state workers.
96.2% of voting members authorized the strike.
The labor board found CalHR refused to meet and confer in good faith.
Mediation resumes Oct. 30.
stories.next: Mediation between SEIU Local 1000 and the state resumes Oct. 30.
stories.left: The union argues that workers who kept California running through the pandemic deserve a raise, affordable health care and flexibility, and that the state broke labor law by refusing to bargain. Supporters say a rested, fairly paid workforce serves the public better than a four-day office mandate.
stories.right: Critics say public-employee strikes hurt residents who need the DMV and parks, and they point to a state budget under strain. They argue return-to-office rules are a reasonable management call and that Newsom's veto of strike benefits reflects limits on what taxpayers can fund.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning coverage of this strike found beyond Fox Business's report on Newsom's earlier veto.

stories.title: U.S. and Israel reportedly plan new Iran strikes after the midterms
stories.summary: Oil jumped on a New York Times report of 'short but intensive' strike plans; Trump says the U.S. is not negotiating.
story: The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterms, unnamed U.S. officials told The New York Times, describing a "short but intensive" operation (CNBC). Brent crude rose about 4 percent to $113.17, its highest since May 4, and reached about $114.5 on Friday morning (CNBC, Fox News).

Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that something "one way or the other" will happen "fairly soon" (CNBC). Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four vessels were struck and caught fire in the Persian Gulf, and Washington ordered non-emergency government staff out of Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate (CNBC). Fox News reported Prime Minister Netanyahu urging the U.S. and Israel to overthrow the Iranian government.
On Oct. 8 Trump had said the U.S. would not attack before the election (Axios, CNN). CNN has reported that the military drafted options including a very large bomb against nuclear and energy sites.
The war began Feb. 28, and oil is more than 45 percent higher since then (NBC News).
facts: The war began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli strikes.
Brent settled at $113.17, the highest since May 4 (CNBC).
Trump pledged Oct. 8 not to strike before the election.
The U.S. ordered non-emergency staff out of Saudi Arabia.
Iran's IRGC says four vessels were struck in the Gulf.
stories.next: Watch for the next Hormuz attacks and any Trump statement before Nov. 3.
stories.left: Critics say planning a strike timed for after the election treats war as a campaign calendar item, and that Congress has not authorized an open-ended conflict. They point to oil above $100 and higher costs at home as proof that escalation has no clear endpoint.
stories.right: Supporters argue that Iran keeps attacking shipping and has mined Hormuz, that the blockade and sanctions pressure are working, and that a short, decisive operation is better than a drifting standoff. Hawks say Tehran will not bargain seriously until it believes force is credible.

stories.title: Putin agrees in principle to resume three-way Ukraine talks after Nov. 10
stories.summary: Witkoff met Putin Oct. 21 and Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard; Kyiv was struck hours later.
story: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21, and Putin agreed in principle to restart three-way talks with Kyiv and Washington after Nov. 10, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said (The Hill). The Kremlin said Abu Dhabi could host the next round, with no date set. Russia also freed American Stephen Hubbard (NBC News).

Hours after the announcement, Russia hit Kyiv with a large missile and drone attack that killed two people and injured 34, Zelensky said (CNN, The Hill). Zelensky wants a meeting by early November and says Moscow has repeatedly promised talks and then canceled.

Zelensky told CNN there is "nothing personal" between him and Trump, though the relationship has soured over a U.S. diesel deal with Russia and sanctions waivers (CNN). Czech President Petr Pavel said the diesel deal derailed progress (The Hill). Zelensky says Ukraine would accept a freeze on the current front line but not give up territory it holds.
Trump says his team is "the closest we've been" to a settlement; the Kremlin said earlier proposals contained little of value.
facts: Witkoff met Putin Oct. 21 in St. Petersburg.
Putin agreed in principle to talks after Nov. 10; Abu Dhabi is a possible venue.
Russia's attack on Kyiv killed two and injured 34.
Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard.
Zelensky would accept a freeze on the front line.
stories.next: No date is set; watch for a Nov. 10-plus meeting announcement.
stories.left: Critics say easing sanctions on Russian diesel rewarded Putin while he kept bombing Kyiv, and that the talks are a stalling tactic. They want more aid to Ukraine and tougher sanctions before any deal that rewards aggression.
stories.right: Supporters argue that only direct engagement with Moscow can end the war, that Europe should carry more of the burden, and that Kyiv must face the reality of the front line. They credit the push for the Hubbard release as a sign diplomacy can work.
stories.blindspot: Little right-leaning coverage of this round turned up in my searches.

stories.title: Oil near $100 and a 5 percent Treasury yield squeeze the economy
stories.summary: WTI sits near $101 and the 10-year yield is 4.98 percent as Iran strike fears lift energy costs.
story: U.S. crude traded above $100 a barrel Friday and Brent hit a five-month high after reports of planned strikes on Iran (CNBC). WTI futures were at $101.24 in the latest live data, and Brent was near $114 (CNBC, Fox News). Oil is more than 45 percent above where it stood when the war began Feb. 28.

The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.98 percent in the latest data, after a stretch above 5 percent. CNBC reported that CoreWeave's market confidence eroded as bond yields spiked, showing how rates are feeding into AI financing.
Higher fuel costs feed inflation, which is why the Federal Reserve has little room to cut. Fox News polling shows voters blaming the economy for inflation.
The next hard data on prices and growth will shape the Fed's path into year-end.
facts: WTI was $101.24 and Brent about $114 in the latest data.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.98%.
Oil is up more than 45% since the war began Feb. 28.
Brent's $113.17 settlement was the highest since May 4.
stories.next: Watch the next oil settlement and 10-year yield around the 5 percent line.
stories.left: Democrats argue that a war of choice drove up gas and heating costs and that voters are paying for it. They call for diplomacy and for investment in clean energy to cut exposure to oil shocks.
stories.right: Republicans argue that the administration's blockade and sanctions are the right pressure on Iran and that more U.S. drilling and pipelines would blunt price swings. They also blame earlier spending for sticky inflation.

stories.title: Nasdaq's worst day since June, then Tesla and SpaceX merger talk
stories.summary: AI funding fears and oil hit tech, while Tesla beat estimates and Musk said SpaceX-Tesla special committees are discussing a merger.
story: The Nasdaq fell 2.60 percent to 26,008.86, its worst day since June, and the S&P 500 lost 1.21 percent to 7,663.43 while the Dow edged up 0.02 percent (CNBC, live data). Futures pointed lower again Thursday night as AI worries and oil above $100 weighed (CNBC).

Tesla reported Q3 adjusted earnings of 48 cents a share against 43 cents expected, on revenue of $28.05 billion against $27.9 billion; auto revenue fell 3 percent to $20.56 billion (CNBC). Shares then slid as analysts focused on spending for emerging projects (CNBC).
SpaceX stock rose 10 percent after its earnings, and Musk said Tesla and SpaceX boards have formed special committees to discuss a merger, calling it a "good idea" (CNBC).
Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28 and Amazon Oct. 29, all after the close.
facts: Nasdaq -2.60%, S&P 500 -1.21%, Dow +0.02% (live data).
Tesla beat on EPS (48c vs 43c) and revenue ($28.05B).
SpaceX rose 10% after earnings.
Alphabet and Microsoft report Oct. 28; Amazon Oct. 29.
stories.next: Big Tech earnings start Oct. 28 with Alphabet and Microsoft.
stories.why: The selloff shows how much the market now depends on AI spending staying financed. With oil and yields both high, earnings from Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon will test whether the spending pays off.

stories.title: IBM's Anderon builds a 300 mm quantum chip foundry with $1 billion in CHIPS money
stories.summary: Commerce finalized an award of up to $1 billion, matched by IBM, for a quantum wafer foundry in Albany.
story: The Commerce Department finalized a CHIPS and Science Act R&D award of up to $1 billion for Anderon, a quantum foundry IBM set up this year, and IBM is matching it with $1 billion in cash plus intellectual property and staff (IEEE Spectrum). Anderon is based in Albany, New York, and will run a 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry.

It builds on work at Albany NanoTech, where IBM has made quantum wafers for more than five years. CEO Mukesh Khare said first wafers are already moving through a production-scale line (IEEE Spectrum).
The award was first reported in May as part of a $2 billion package for nine quantum companies in which the government takes minority equity stakes (CNBC, Bloomberg).
The pitch is a fabless model for quantum chips: other companies design qubit devices and a dedicated fab builds them, as classical chip foundries do.
facts: Award: up to $1 billion from CHIPS and Science Act funds.
IBM is matching with $1 billion in cash.
The fab uses 300 mm wafers in Albany, New York.
The government takes a minority equity stake (CNBC).
stories.next: Watch for the first outside design customers for Anderon wafers.
stories.why: Quantum chips are mostly built in small labs. A shared, standard fab could cut costs and speed up designs the way foundries did for classical chips.
stories.flag: Sources disagree on the exact date of the final award; IEEE Spectrum dates it Sept. 16.

stories.title: Applied Materials opens $5 billion EPIC Center in Sunnyvale
stories.summary: The facility puts TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix in one building with equipment makers and universities.
story: Applied Materials opened its EPIC Center in Sunnyvale on Oct. 12, calling it the world's largest facility for collaborative semiconductor process and equipment R&D, with $5 billion in planned investment as customer projects start (Applied Materials, Evertiq). It has nearly four acres of cleanroom space.

Founding partners are TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix. Broadcom, Advantest, SCREEN, KIOXIA and Besi are innovation partners, and Arizona State, RPI, Stanford, UC Berkeley and UCLA are research partners (Applied Materials).
CEO Gary Dickerson framed it as part of the race for AI leadership, and Applied says working side by side could cut years off the path from concept to commercial production.
IEEE Spectrum has tied it to a wave of AI-driven semiconductor R&D spending.
facts: Opened Oct. 12 in Sunnyvale, California.
Planned investment: $5 billion over time.
Founding partners: TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix.
About four acres of cleanroom space.
stories.next: Watch for the first announced joint projects from the partners.
stories.why: Putting chipmakers and toolmakers together early is meant to shorten the time to new chip processes, and it keeps this work in the Bay Area.

stories.title: NASA's Roman telescope enters final commissioning
stories.summary: Engineers say the observatory and its primary instrument are working; first images are expected in early 2027.
story: NASA says its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has entered its final commissioning phase after a checkout of the observatory and its primary instrument, and engineers say it is fully functional (NASA). Roman launched on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy on Aug. 30 (Space.com, Astronomy).

After commissioning and calibration, first images are expected in early 2027 (Space.com). The wide-field instrument's image quality and the coronagraph's light-blocking performance have not yet been verified in space.
Roman is built to survey large areas of sky for dark energy, exoplanets and distant galaxies.
facts: Launched Aug. 30 on a Falcon Heavy.
NASA reports the observatory and primary instrument are fully functional.
First images are expected in early 2027.
Wide-field imaging and coronagraph performance are not yet verified in space.
stories.next: Watch for first-light images in early 2027.
stories.why: Roman's wide view lets it map far more sky than Hubble, which matters for dark energy and exoplanet surveys.

stories.title: NASA holds Artemis III update today
stories.summary: A 2 p.m. ET briefing covers Artemis III, a 2027 crewed Earth-orbit test with two lunar landers.
story: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other officials hold an "Artemis Acceleration" briefing at 2 p.m. ET today on Artemis III, which will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit and test docking with commercial landers (Space.com). I found no report of the briefing yet.

Artemis III is targeted for the third quarter of 2027. Orion would dock with Blue Moon for about two days, then with SpaceX's Starship for about a day without the crew entering it. The crew is Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano, Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (Space.com).
Booster stacking finished Sept. 30, and Isaacman wants a wet dress rehearsal before year's end (NASA, Space.com). A crewed lunar landing would follow on Artemis IV in 2028.
Schedule shifts from Starship and Blue Moon delays have moved the dates.
facts: Artemis III is targeted for Q3 2027.
The crew is Bresnik, Parmitano, Douglas and Rubio.
Booster stacking was completed Sept. 30.
Artemis IV would attempt a crewed landing in 2028.
stories.next: Today's 2 p.m. ET briefing; a wet dress rehearsal is targeted by year's end.
stories.why: Artemis III tests the docking steps a lunar landing needs, so its schedule sets the date for Americans returning to the Moon.
stories.flag: Outcome of today's briefing is not yet reported.

stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet, an always-on agent app
stories.summary: The research-preview app watches connected apps and sends a daily brief, built on Claude Opus 5.5.
story: Anthropic announced Claude Duet on Oct. 21, a standalone agent app for professionals and small-business owners that monitors connected apps and flags items needing attention instead of waiting for prompts (Reuters via KFGO, TechCrunch). It sends a morning brief and messages users only when something needs attention.

It runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and uses the connectors in the Claude Marketplace, which Reuters puts at more than 6,000 (Reuters via KFGO). Users can hand it tasks by text or voice in one thread, from scheduling to building dashboards or prototypes.

It is a waitlisted research preview on iOS, Android and claude.ai for U.S. Pro and Max subscribers. Anthropic acknowledges it can misjudge urgency and asks for approval before sensitive actions (Reuters via KFGO).
Coverage frames it as a response to OpenAI's Dots, Meta's Muse and similar always-on agents (iPhone in Canada).
facts: Announced Oct. 21; research preview.
Built on Claude Opus 5.5.
Available to U.S. Pro and Max subscribers by waitlist.
Asks for approval before sensitive actions.
stories.next: Watch the waitlist rollout and how it handles urgency calls in early use.
stories.why: Moving from chat to always-on agents shifts AI from tool to assistant. The hard parts are trust, permissions and false alarms.
stories.flag: Reports differ on whether the announcement was Wednesday or Thursday.

stories.title: OpenAI brings its models to Google Cloud
stories.summary: OpenAI will sell models on Google's cloud, putting them on all three major U.S. clouds.
story: OpenAI will bring its AI models to Google's cloud, expanding beyond Microsoft and putting its models on the three major U.S. clouds (CNBC, Oct. 21). Developers will be able to reach them through Google's cloud tools.

The move follows an April amendment that ended Microsoft's exclusive hosting. Microsoft stays the primary cloud partner and OpenAI products ship first on Azure, while OpenAI can serve customers on any cloud (9to5Google).
Reports say Microsoft no longer shares revenue on OpenAI products it sells and keeps its IP license through 2032 (Khaleej Times).
facts: Announced Oct. 21 by CNBC's report.
April amendment ended Microsoft's exclusivity.
Microsoft remains primary cloud partner.
Microsoft's IP license runs through 2032.
stories.next: Watch Alphabet's Oct. 28 earnings for cloud commentary.
stories.why: More clouds mean more compute for OpenAI and more leverage against any single provider, and they raise the stakes for Google Cloud's AI revenue.
stories.flag: Terms of the Google Cloud arrangement are not detailed in sources I found.

stories.title: CoreWeave's slide tests the AI financing chain
stories.summary: CoreWeave is down 36 percent in October as bond yields rise and Nvidia's CEO says it needs no backstop.
story: CoreWeave's market value is about $31 billion, down from a peak near $90 billion, and its stock is down 36 percent this month at about $61.82, below the price Nvidia paid in January (CNBC, Oct. 21). Its unsecured debt yields about 15 percent.

Nvidia owns about 9 percent of CoreWeave. On Oct. 15, Jensen Huang told Bloomberg Nvidia need not backstop the company, saying its cost of capital is decreasing, and neocloud shares rebounded that day (Bloomberg). Some investors say further Nvidia support may still be needed.
Nvidia, AMD and Dell fell in a global tech rout on AI funding worries that day (CNBC). Mizuho's Jordan Klein called Nvidia's neocloud bets more questionable.
The same worry hit the Nasdaq this week.
facts: CoreWeave market value is about $31 billion.
The stock is down 36% in October.
Nvidia holds about 9% of CoreWeave.
CoreWeave's unsecured debt yields about 15%.
stories.next: Nvidia reports Nov. 18; Big Tech capex guidance comes Oct. 28-29.
stories.why: A lot of AI data-center building runs on debt. If lenders get nervous, the chain from chipmakers to cloud builders can tighten fast.

stories.title: mRNA melanoma vaccine cuts recurrence risk 42 percent in late-stage trial
stories.summary: Merck and Moderna say the personalized vaccine plus Keytruda beat Keytruda alone; full data come Saturday.
story: Merck and Moderna said their personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine, intismeran autogene, combined with Keytruda cut the risk of melanoma returning or death by 42 percent versus Keytruda alone in a late-stage trial (CNN, Oct. 22). Full data will be presented Saturday in Madrid at the ESMO meeting.

The companies said in August that the INTerpath-001 trial met its main goal of recurrence-free survival and a secondary goal on spread of the cancer. It enrolled 1,137 patients with resected stage IIB-IV melanoma (SCMP, CNN).

Earlier smaller trials showed larger effects: 44 percent in a 2022 Phase 2b study and 49 percent at three years (CNN). Those data were preliminary and not peer reviewed. The companies say they are "engaging with regulatory authorities."
No FDA filing date has been given.
facts: Result: 42% lower risk of recurrence or death.
Trial size: 1,137 patients.
Full data presented Saturday at ESMO in Madrid.
No FDA filing date announced.
stories.next: Full data at ESMO in Madrid on Saturday, Oct. 24.
stories.why: This is the first big Phase 3 test of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, so the result will shape the field.
stories.flag: The 42 percent figure comes from CNN's report of company results; the data are not yet published.

briefs: CNN reports a mutated H1N1 strain is driving an early flu season on the West Coast, though national flu-like visits remain below baseline (CNN).
Replit's CEO said ChatGPT is now its default over Anthropic, though insiders disputed that the partnership ended (TechCrunch).
Treasury added sanctions on 17 vessels it calls part of an Iranian shadow fleet (The Hill).
